stages.title: Price elasticity of supply
stages.sub: After this, the student can measure and explain how responsive supply is to price changes, and why time matters.

steps.q: A furniture maker plots how many chairs they are willing and able to sell at £50, £80 and £120. What have they just plotted?
steps.right: The quantities they would supply at each price
steps.wrong: The quantities customers would buy at each price
steps.hint: Whose decision is this: the seller's or the buyer's?

steps.q: A new law now requires expensive safety checks on all chair timber. The maker offers fewer chairs at every single price than before. Did price cause this, or something else?
steps.hint: Look at each price on the old curve: has the quantity offered at that same price changed?

steps.q: Chair price rises from £50 to £60 and quantity offered rises from 100 to 105. To compare how big each change was relative to its starting point, what would you turn both changes into?
steps.right: A proportion of the original figure, shown as a percentage
steps.wrong: The plain difference in pounds and in chairs
steps.hint: £10 and 5 chairs are not directly comparable units. What common measure would let you compare them fairly?
steps.pre: Turning each change into a proportion of its starting value gives you a

steps.q: Using those two proportions, quantity supplied rose by 5% when price rose by 20%. What single number would you calculate to summarise this?
steps.right: The percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price
steps.wrong: The percentage change in price divided by the percentage change in quantity
steps.hint: You want to know how much quantity responds per unit of price change, so which one is on top?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: For the chairs, a 20% price rise led to only a 5% rise in quantity supplied, giving a ratio of 0.25. Is quantity supplied responding strongly or weakly to price?
steps.hint: 0.25 is less than 1. Is the top number bigger or smaller than the bottom number?

steps.q: A bakery can hire another cook and buy more flour within a day to make far more bread when price rises. A vineyard cannot grow new grapes any faster than one harvest a year. Which one can adjust output more easily?
steps.hint: Think about how quickly each producer can get hold of extra resources to raise output.

steps.q: Right after a price rise, the vineyard has no more grapes to sell, but a year later it has planted extra vines and expanded output. Was the vineyard's supply more responsive to price straight away, or later on?
steps.right: Later on, once more time had passed
steps.wrong: Straight away, before anything could change
steps.hint: Compare what the vineyard could do on day one against what it could do after a full growing season.
